newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX gasoline ends higher on Citgo refinery blast.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX gasoline ends higher on Citgo refinery blast.

text.p: NYMEX gasoline settled higher on Tuesday after a blast at a 132,500 barrel per day Citgo refinery disrupted production.
A fire after the blast at the Corpus Christi, Texas refinery Monday night occurred in the alkylation unit and has shut that and other units at the plant, a spokesman for the company said.
But, dealers downplayed the event saying not much production was disrupted at a time when the market was already bracing for more supply.
"It actually is not all that much that was taken down, so I am surprised that it settled up at all," said a New York products trader.
Production at the alkylation unit has a rated capacity of 21,000 barrels per day (bpd), the official said.
Meanwhile, Tosco Corp has told local residents in Trainer, Pennsylvania that its 150,000 bpd is being tested prior to full operation.
The plant is expected to add about 100,000 bpd to the Atlantic basin gasoline market.
Also countering the bullish Citgo news was a general consolidation in oil prices sparked by spot crude's rising more than $1.00 intraday on Monday.
Oil prices are expected to continue the consolidation Wednesday following the release of bearish oil inventory data from the American Petroleum Institute (API).

"We are going to test $20.55 barrel. If we break that, then we are back to the $19.50 to $20.50 range," said Bob MacMinn, president of MPAS Inc, a petroleum consulting firm in Toronto in response to the API report.

The API said gasoline stocks grew a surprising 6.51 million barrels for the May 9 week when traders had expected a build of only a one million barrels. Moreover, gasoline production rose to 8.1 million barrels per day (bpd) from 7.7 million bpd.
Gasoline production was spurred on by a sharp rise in refinery run rates that stood at a feverish 96.9 percent versus 94.5 percent last week.
Despite the high run rates and lower imports, crude stocks grew 6.94 million barrels compared to a build expected by traders of less than one million barrels.

Distillate stocks dropped 1.10 million barrels when dealers had expected a build, but because distillate stocks include heating oil which is out of season, dealers were expected to shrug off the draw.
-- Hary Milling, New York Energy Desk, 212-859-1761
